Dear all,

I have a question and I owe you a debt of gratitude if you could help me out in this regard. Also, I should mention that I’m newbie in Stan and maybe it is a dumb question. My question is as following:

 

Let's say N (x | g <= 0 ) is my target distribution. (Bivariate normal space)
g = B - ((1/√n) * Σ xi) is my limit state function, where B = 3 , n (problem dimension) = 2 and as i mentioned xi or x have a bivariate standard normal distribution. (i = 1,2 because the n is 2)

How can i model this target distribution in Stan?

I used the indicator function to involve the g into my target distribution

Is my following Stan code correct?

Thank you very much in advance for your help.


data {
  int<lower=0> n;
}
parameters {
  vector[2] x;
}
model {
real g;
    int I[n];

//limit state function
g = 3 - (sum(x)/sqrt(2));

//likelihood
if (g > 0){
            I[n]=0; //Indicator function
        }else{
            I[n]=1;
        }

  x ~ normal(0, 1)*I[n];
}

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Newbie in Stan; likelihood with indicator function
parts:
Hamed,

You are confusing the target distribution with the expectation that you want
to take.

If you want to define the target distribution as being zero for g <= 0 then
you have to specify a truncated distribution which may require a normalizing
constant. There is discussion of this in the manual. Note that outside of
one dimension, truncated distributions are hard to derive analytically.

On the other hand, it looks like you’re trying to compute the expectation
of I[g > 0] with respect to an IID gaussian target distribution (i.e. the probability
of g > 0). In that case you want to compute the indicator in generated
quantities,

parameters {
vector[2] x;
}

model {

x ~ normal(0, 1);
}

generated quantities {
int I = 0;
{
real g = 3 - (sum(x)/sqrt(2));
if (g > 0) I = 1;
}
}

Then the average of I across your chain will be P[g > 0].

But as we keep trying to tell you, if it's Gaussian, you can

you have non-data arguments to the normal, then you need to write something
like:

a ~ normal(mu, sigma) T[a, b];

parts:
Hamed,

No, you are not understanding how all of this works.
Probability can be very subtle and we highly encourage
you to work through the basics before trying to tackle
trickier problems like this.

If you want to sample from a truncated distribution
efficiently then you’ll have to evaluate the integral

\int_{invalid neighborhood(hyper params) d(params) pi(params, hyperparams)

analytically.  We can do this for univariate densities,
thence the discussion in the manual.  But we cannot
in general do this for multivariate densities, even if
your target is a truncated multivariate Gaussian.

The best you can hope for is that the truncating
boundary is a plane so that you can rotate your
system such that the truncation lies alone one
axis only and your and the integral analytically.
For nonlinear truncations the problem will in
general be intractable.

On Saturday, April 29, 2017 at 9:45:41 PM UTC-4, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Hamed,

No, you are not understanding how all of this works.
Probability can be very subtle and we highly encourage
you to work through the basics before trying to tackle
trickier problems like this.

If you want to sample from a truncated distribution
efficiently then you’ll have to evaluate the integral

\int_{invalid neighborhood(hyper params) d(params) pi(params, hyperparams)

analytically.  We can do this for univariate densities,
thence the discussion in the manual.  But we cannot
in general do this for multivariate densities, even if
your target is a truncated multivariate Gaussian.

The best you can hope for is that the truncating
boundary is a plane so that you can rotate your
system such that the truncation lies alone one
axis only and your and the integral analytically.
For nonlinear truncations the problem will in
general be intractable.
